lesson.title: Who sees and who speaks

steps.headline: Grammatical person tells you where the narrator stands.

lead.text: A first-person narrator is a character who says “I”, as Poe's does. A third-person narrator stands outside the story and calls the characters “he” and “she”. An omniscient third-person narrator can also generalise beyond any one mind.
Emma opens with a narrator who describes its heroine. Ask whether the narrator ever speaks as a character, and notice how much the word “seemed” suggests it knows.

reveal.text: Third person: the narrator names Emma and calls her “she”. “Seemed” already hints that this narrator knows more than Emma does. Poe's narrator, by contrast, says “why will you say that I am mad?”

spans.text: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence;
True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?

lead.text: An omniscient narrator can generalise beyond any one mind. Pride and Prejudice opens with a claim about what is “universally acknowledged”. Ask who is speaking, and whose assumption it is.

reveal.text: The narrator voices a neighbourhood's assumption with irony. The next paragraph shows the “surrounding families” regarding a rich newcomer as “the rightful property” of their daughters, so the wanting runs the other way.

spans.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged,
that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.
this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as
of some one or other of their daughters.

steps.headline: Free indirect discourse puts a character's thought into the narrator's grammar.

lead.text: The narrator keeps third person and past tense, but the character's exclamation, question or idiom enters the sentence with no “she thought that”. There are no quotation marks, so the reader moves between minds without a signal.

steps.headline: Turn Anna's thought “What a dreadful day this has been!” into free indirect discourse.

workedSteps.text: Start from the direct thought, in her words and her person: “What a dreadful day this has been!”
Move to the narrator's grammar: third person and past tense.
Keep her exclamation and drop the reporting words. “What a dreadful day it had been!”

lead.text: After Mr Elton's proposal, Austen writes: “Emma sat down to think and be miserable. It was a wretched business indeed!” The second sentence is Emma's exclamation, not the narrator's verdict.

reveal.text: The narrator's grammar carries Emma's voice, so readers share her mistakes before they recognise them as mistakes.

spans.text: The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
It was a wretched business indeed!
“If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
How she could have been so deceived!

lead.text: Two questions sort the modes: who is speaking, and whose words are these? Quotation marks mark direct speech. Actions reported from outside are plain narration.

reveal.text: “How she could have been so deceived!” is Emma's exclamation in the narrator's third person and past tense. No reporting verb or quotation marks frame it.

spans.text: (1) “If I had not persuaded Harriet into liking the man, I could have borne any thing.”
(2) The hair was curled, and the maid sent away, and Emma sat down to think and be miserable.
(3) How she could have been so deceived!
Such an overthrow of every thing she had been wishing for!
She looked back as well as she could;

lesson.orientation: Distinguish first- from third-person narration and hear an omniscient narrator's irony. Recognise free indirect discourse in Austen.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh text after a delay.

blocks.text: Two friends retell the same awkward entrance, one saying “I” and the other “she”.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell first- from third-person narration and spot free indirect discourse in Austen.

recap.keyIdea: A narrator's grammatical person fixes where they stand. Free indirect discourse lets a character's own voice speak inside the narrator's third person.

blocks.text: You saw Emma's narrator stand outside the story and heard Austen's irony in the neighbourhood's voice. You also picked out Emma's exclamation as free indirect discourse in a third-person sentence.

recap.nextHook: Voices can mean the opposite of what they say. Next: verbal, dramatic and situational irony.

questions.prompt: Austen opens Emma: 'Emma Woodhouse … seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence.' In which grammatical person is this narration?
hints: Does the narrator say 'I', or describe Emma from outside?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Third person: the narrator names Emma and refers to her as 'she', standing outside the story.

questions.onCorrect: Third person: the narrator names Emma and calls her “she”, standing outside the story.

misconceptions.feedback: First person means the narrator says “I”. Does this narrator?
Second person addresses the reader as “you”. This narrator describes someone else.

questions.onCorrect: The narrator states the assumption as universal, and the next paragraph shows it belongs to families with daughters to marry.

questions.prompt: After Mr Elton's proposal Austen writes: 'Emma sat down to think and be miserable. It was a wretched business indeed!' The second sentence is Emma's own exclamation, in the third person and past tense, with no 'she thought' and no quotation marks. What is this technique called?
hints: Compare it with 'She thought that it was a wretched business'. Which part has been dropped, and what does that make the reported thought?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Free indirect discourse, also called free indirect style or speech: the narrator's grammar carries the character's voice.

questions.onCorrect: Free indirect discourse: the narrator's grammar carries the character's voice, with no reporting verb.

misconceptions.feedback: Indirect speech keeps the reporting words: “she thought that”. Here they have been dropped.
Direct speech would use quotation marks and the character's own person.

hints: Direct speech sits inside quotation marks.

questions.prompt: A friend retells her day: “I walked in and everyone went quiet.” Where is she in relation to the story?

acceptedIdeas: She is a character in it.
